description:
Lightweight, private Windows system monitor.

Vitals shows what is slowing your computer down, in plain language: CPU, GPU, memory, disks,
network, temperatures and per-process usage, with history, alerts and a compact overlay.
Optional read-only access from your phone on the local network. No account, no telemetry.
Added
- AI page: a session now shows what it actually used — input, output, cached
  and reasoning tokens, the number of requests, the output speed in tokens per
  second, the time to the first token and the cost — wherever the client
  records them. Copilot CLI sessions stop reading as an em dash; VS Code
  Copilot Chat sessions say the client records no usage instead. The Insights
  tab gains the same numbers as a page total (ADR 0043).
- Alerts you write yourself: pick a reading (CPU, CPU temperature, memory, disk
  activity, battery, dropped packets), a side of a threshold and how long it
  has to hold, and Vitals watches it. The window and the cooldown are per
  rule, so "CPU above 90% for 30 seconds" means that at every sampling rate.
- Alert destinations: a webhook, an ntfy topic, a Discord webhook or a Home
  Assistant instance, each alert routed to the ones you choose, with a Test
  button per destination. A webhook is signed with HMAC so your endpoint can
  verify the sender. Nothing is sent until you add an address.
- "Is it my PC, my router or my internet?" — a probe in the diagnosis dialog,
  on a button, that sends four echo requests to the router and to two public
  addresses and says which of the three is at fault. Also available to a paired
  phone over the LAN (GET /api/v1/connectivity) so the answer is on the phone
  too.
- A service that was running and stopped is now an alert, and one you stopped
  yourself in Vitals is not.
- The watchdog checks GitHub once a day and says so when a newer Vitals exists,
  which covers the machine where the app itself is not running. It only looks:
  nothing is downloaded and nothing is installed from there.
- The tray icon can carry a reading — CPU, CPU temperature, memory or network
  traffic — instead of the plain mark. Off by default, and free when off: no
  value is computed and no bitmap drawn.
- Health: connect Vitals to your vmui account and see your own health and
  nutrition summary on the desktop, iPhone and Android. Held in memory only,
  never written to disk; the page stays hidden until you connect.
- Apple Watch: a companion inside the iPhone app shows the PC you are
  watching on your wrist, fed by the phone.
- Mac App Store edition ("Vitals Monitor"): sandboxed and built without the
  self-updater, so updates come from the App Store. It cannot see other
  apps' processes or the temperature sensors, and says so.
Changed
- The controls that only exist on Windows are hidden elsewhere rather than
  shown and failing: the navigation, the command palette, the process menu and
  the Settings rows all ask the backend what this machine can do.
- Dialogs, menus, tooltips and sheets animate in and out. They did not before:
  the overlay style was a CSS transition while the layer that unmounts them
  waits for an animation, so every overlay was removed in the same tick it
  was closed.
- The AI agents page now names the service Kodwen, its new name after the
  November 2026 rebrand, and speaks to ai.kodwen.com and auth.kodwen.com
  instead of ai.codai.ro and auth.codai.ro. A key stored by an earlier
  version is moved to the new Credential Manager entry on first use, so
  nobody is signed out by the update. The old hosts still work, so an
  un-updated build keeps signing in during the changeover (ADR 0042).

The Android downloads are the github flavour — the one allowed to scan
folders; the Play builds have no all-files access.
Verifying this download
Windows may show a SmartScreen warning on first run (Windows protected your
PC) because the installer is not yet signed with a commercial certificate.
Choose More info → Run anyway. That is expected — see
docs/distribution.md.
You do not have to take our word for what is in the binary. With the
GitHub CLI:
gh attestation verify .\Vitals_x64-setup.exe --repo dragoscv/vitals
This proves the file was built by this repository's release workflow from the
tagged commit, and nowhere else. Checksums for every file are in
SHA256SUMS.txt:
(Get-FileHash .\Vitals_x64-setup.exe -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower()
Software bills of materials (CycloneDX) for the Rust and JavaScript
dependencies are attached as sbom-rust.cdx.json and sbom-js.cdx.json,
and one for the command-line tool as sbom-cli.cdx.json.
